To fix (4)

To fix Marginal Significance

What we found

You described 3 effects with terms related to ‘marginally significant’.

Show details

You described effects with terms related to ‘marginally significant’. If p values above 0.05 are interpreted as an effect, you inflate the alpha level, and increase the Type 1 error rate. If a p value is higher than the prespecified alpha level, it should be interpreted as a non-significant result.

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 1 imprecise p value out of 51 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text
p < .10 10 †.05 ≤ p < .10; p<.05; p<.01; p<.001.11 12 13 Hopeful sentiment Negative-human Information-seeking intentions Anxious sentiment Positive-human Positive-animal Negative-animal .08 † -.08* -.15** .09* .21** .37*** .07 † Participants’ message selections (selective exposure)

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 16 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

README Files

README files are a way to document the contents and structure of a folder, helping users locate the information they need. You can use a README to document changes to a repository, and explain how files are named. Please consider adding a README to each repository or including ‘README’ in the name of your overview document.

Registration Points to a Closed Project

1 OSF project (https://osf.io/zfpv8) is referenced by a registration in this manuscript, but it is closed or inaccessible, and no copy of its files could be found anywhere else. Some OSF registrations only describe what was shared, while the actual files live in the project they were registered from — if that project is closed and the registration holds no copy, metacheck cannot list or download its files, and other researchers cannot access them either. Consider making the source project openly available, or re-uploading its files directly into the registration.

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). install.packages() calls were found in 2 code files.

File name install.packages() calls found
Study 1_Main Analysis.R install.packages(pkg, dependencies = TRUE)
Study 2_Main Analysis.R install.packages(pkg, dependencies = TRUE)

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In all code files, libraries/imports were loaded in one block.

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 10 distinct packages/libraries: broom, car, dplyr, emmeans, ggplot2, lavaan, lme4, patchwork, psych, tibble. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).

Reproducible Environment

No renv.lock file, sessionInfo()/session_info() record, or groundhog/checkpoint date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an renv.lock (via the renv package), a sessionInfo() text dump, or a groundhog/checkpoint date-pin alongside the code.

Parsable code

All R-type code files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd) could be read in. There were no parsing issues.

To check Data Check

What we found

  • We classified 8 files: 2 data, 3 code, 2 documentation, 1 materials.
  • We found 2 tabular data files and extracted 160 columns from 2 of them.
  • We grouped the files into 2 study groups (ex1, ex2). We ran automated data-quality checks on 160 columns and found no issues. 171 survey respondents were flagged for possible careless responding (171 of them only via short-scale straightlining, which can be normal answering). We detected demographic columns for Age, Gender.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 160 columns across 2 data files.

Careless Responding

171 distinct respondents were flagged for straightlining: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is one row per person, and the Longest run column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, 171 were flagged only by short-scale straightlining (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.

These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

What this does not cover. Only 1 of 2 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

A script runs longer than our limit of 5 minutes.

  • Study 2_Main Analysis.R

State in the README how long each script runs. If some steps take hours, save their results (such as fitted models) to files, add those to the deposit, and let the script read them, so readers can check the rest without waiting.

Comparison with the paper

Of the 75 statistical tests reported in the paper, 55 were found in the output of the code.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 3 R code files.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), source() calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

Order File Runs after Basis
1 Study 1_Main Analysis.R — numeric
2 Study1_Power Analysis.R — numeric
3 Study 2_Main Analysis.R — numeric

File paths

Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 3 scripts: 2 ran without error, 0 errored, 1 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

File Outcome Detail Time (s)
Study 1_Main Analysis.R ran_ok 212.0
Study1_Power Analysis.R ran_ok 242.0
Study 2_Main Analysis.R timed_out timeout 300.4

Calls that install packages in the code

2 calls to install.packages(), groundhog, checkpoint, renv, pacman and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: groundhog.library() and p_load() by library(), the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.

> parallel_model <- '
>   # Paths to mediators 
>   post_env_hope ~ a1*choice01 + a2*choice02 + a3*choice03 + a4*choice04 +
>                          pre_env_hope + pre_env_anxiety + 
>                          pre_env_interest + pre_env_urgency + pre_env_knowledge
> 
>   post_env_anxiety ~ a5*choice01 + a6*choice02 + a7*choice03 + a8*choice04 +
>                          pre_env_hope + pre_env_anxiety + 
>                          pre_env_interest + pre_env_urgency + pre_env_knowledge
> 
>   # Paths to outcome 
>   seeking_env ~ b1*post_env_hope + b2*post_env_anxiety +
>                    c1*choice01 + c2*choice02 + c3*choice03 + c4*choice04 +
>                    pre_env_hope + pre_env_anxiety + 
>                    pre_env_interest + pre_env_urgency + pre_env_knowledge
> 
>   # Indirect effects via hopeful sentiment
>   ind_hope_choice01 := a1 * b1
>   ind_hope_choice02 := a2 * b1
>   ind_hope_choice03 := a3 * b1
>   ind_hope_choice04 := a4 * b1
> 
>   # Indirect effects via anxious sentiment
>   ind_anxiety_choice01 := a5 * b2
>   ind_anxiety_choice02 := a6 * b2
>   ind_anxiety_choice03 := a7 * b2
>   ind_anxiety_choice04 := a8 * b2
>   
>   # Total indirect effects
>   total_ind_choice01 := ind_hope_choice01 + ind_anxiety_choice01
>   total_ind_choice02 := ind_hope_choice02 + ind_anxiety_choice02
>   total_ind_choice03 := ind_hope_choice03 + ind_anxiety_choice03
>   total_ind_choice04 := ind_hope_choice04 + ind_anxiety_choice04
>   
>   # Total effects
>   total_effect_choice01 := c1 + total_ind_choice01
>   total_effect_choice02 := c2 + total_ind_choice02
>   total_effect_choice03 := c3 + total_ind_choice03
>   total_effect_choice04 := c4 + total_ind_choice04
>     
>   # Residual covariance between mediators
>   post_env_hope ~~ post_env_anxiety
> '
> set.seed(1234)
> fit <- lavaan::sem(
>   parallel_model,
>   data = data_std,
>   se = "bootstrap",
>   bootstrap = 5000
> )
> summary(
>   fit,

> library(lavaan)
> library(ggplot2)
> monte_carlo_power_curve <- function(Ns, sims = 1000, alpha = 0.05) {
>   
>   # Effect sizes based on assumed standardized path coefficients
>   a1 <- -0.15
>   b1 <- 0.21
>   a2 <- 0.09
>   b2 <- 0.37
>   c_prime <- 0.01
>   
>   # Lavaan parallel mediation model
>   model <- '
>     M1 ~ a1*X
>     M2 ~ a2*X
>     Y ~ b1*M1 + b2*M2 + c*X
> 
>     ind1 := a1*b1
>     ind2 := a2*b2
>   '
>   
>   results <- list()
>   
>   for (n in Ns) {
>     
>     sig_ind1 <- 0
>     sig_ind2 <- 0
>     
>     for (i in 1:sims) {
>       
>       # Simulate data
>       X <- rnorm(n, 0, 1)
>       M1 <- a1 * X + rnorm(n, 0, 1)
>       M2 <- a2 * X + rnorm(n, 0, 1)
>       Y <- b1 * M1 + b2 * M2 + c_prime * X + rnorm(n, 0, 1)
>       
>       dat <- data.frame(X, M1, M2, Y)
>       
>       # Fit mediation model
>       fit <- tryCatch({
>         lavaan::sem(model, data = dat, fixed.x = FALSE)
>       }, error = function(e) NULL)
>       
>       if (!is.null(fit)) {
>         pe <- lavaan::parameterEstimates(fit)
>         
>         p_ind1 <- pe$pvalue[pe$label == "ind1"]
>         p_ind2 <- pe$pvalue[pe$label == "ind2"]
>         
>         if (length(p_ind1) == 1 && p_ind1 < alpha) sig_ind1 <- sig_ind1 + 1
>         if (length(p_ind2) == 1 && p_ind2 < alpha) sig_ind2 <- sig_ind2 + 1
>       }
>     }
>     
>     results[[as.character(n)]] <- data.frame(
>       N = n,
>       power_ind1 = sig_ind1 / sims,
>       power_ind2 = sig_ind2 / sims
>     )
>   }
>   
>   return(do.call(rbind, results))
> }
> set.seed(123)

>   group_by(domain, valence, relevance) %>%
>   summarise(
>     n = sum(!is.na(choice)),
>     M = mean(choice, na.rm = TRUE),
>     SD = sd(choice, na.rm = TRUE),
>     SE = SD / sqrt(n),
>     CI_low = M - qt(.975, df = n - 1) * SE,
>     CI_high = M + qt(.975, df = n - 1) * SE,
>     .groups = "drop"
>   ) %>%
>   mutate(
>     label = sprintf("%.2f\n(%.2f)", M, SD)
>   )

> parallel_model <- '
>   # Paths to mediators 
>   post_env_hope ~ a1*choice01 + a2*choice02 + a3*choice03 + a4*choice04 +
>                          pre_env_hope + pre_env_anxiety + 
>                          pre_env_interest + pre_env_urgency + pre_env_knowledge
> 
>   post_env_anxiety ~ a5*choice01 + a6*choice02 + a7*choice03 + a8*choice04 +
>                          pre_env_hope + pre_env_anxiety + 
>                          pre_env_interest + pre_env_urgency + pre_env_knowledge
> 
>   # Paths to outcome 
>   seeking_env ~ b1*post_env_hope + b2*post_env_anxiety +
>                    c1*choice01 + c2*choice02 + c3*choice03 + c4*choice04 +
>                    pre_env_hope + pre_env_anxiety + 
>                    pre_env_interest + pre_env_urgency + pre_env_knowledge
> 
>   # Indirect effects via hopeful sentiment
>   ind_hope_choice01 := a1 * b1
>   ind_hope_choice02 := a2 * b1
>   ind_hope_choice03 := a3 * b1
>   ind_hope_choice04 := a4 * b1
> 
>   # Indirect effects via anxious sentiment
>   ind_anxiety_choice01 := a5 * b2
>   ind_anxiety_choice02 := a6 * b2
>   ind_anxiety_choice03 := a7 * b2
>   ind_anxiety_choice04 := a8 * b2
>   
>   # Total indirect effects
>   total_ind_choice01 := ind_hope_choice01 + ind_anxiety_choice01
>   total_ind_choice02 := ind_hope_choice02 + ind_anxiety_choice02
>   total_ind_choice03 := ind_hope_choice03 + ind_anxiety_choice03
>   total_ind_choice04 := ind_hope_choice04 + ind_anxiety_choice04
>   
>   # Total effects
>   total_effect_choice01 := c1 + total_ind_choice01
>   total_effect_choice02 := c2 + total_ind_choice02
>   total_effect_choice03 := c3 + total_ind_choice03
>   total_effect_choice04 := c4 + total_ind_choice04
>     
>   # Residual covariance between mediators
>   post_env_hope ~~ post_env_anxiety
> '
> set.seed(1234)
> fit <- lavaan::sem(
>   parallel_model,
>   data = data_std,
>   se = "bootstrap",
>   bootstrap = 5000
> )
> summary(
>   fit,
>   standardized = TRUE,
>   fit.measures = TRUE,
>   ci = TRUE

> parallel_model_demo <- '
>   # Message-choice paths to the two sentiment variables
>   post_env_hope ~ a1*choice01 + a2*choice02 + a3*choice03 + a4*choice04 + 
>                       pre_env_hope + pre_env_anxiety + 
>                       pre_env_interest + pre_env_urgency + pre_env_knowledge + 
>                       Age + Gender2 + GenderOther + Education_z
>                       
>   post_env_anxiety ~ a5*choice01 + a6*choice02 + a7*choice03 + a8*choice04 + 
>                       pre_env_hope + pre_env_anxiety + 
>                       pre_env_interest + pre_env_urgency + pre_env_knowledge + 
>                       Age + Gender2 + GenderOther + Education_z
> 
>   # Sentiment and direct message-choice paths to information-seeking intention
>   seeking_env ~ b1*post_env_hope + b2*post_env_anxiety + 
>                       c1*choice01 + c2*choice02 + c3*choice03 + c4*choice04 + 
>                       pre_env_hope + pre_env_anxiety + 
>                       pre_env_interest + pre_env_urgency + pre_env_knowledge + 
>                       Age + Gender2 + GenderOther + Education_z
> 
>   # Specific indirect associations via hopeful and anxious sentiments
>   ind_hope_choice01 := a1*b1
>   ind_hope_choice02 := a2*b1
>   ind_hope_choice03 := a3*b1
>   ind_hope_choice04 := a4*b1
>   ind_anxiety_choice01 := a5*b2
>   ind_anxiety_choice02 := a6*b2
>   ind_anxiety_choice03 := a7*b2
>   ind_anxiety_choice04 := a8*b2
> 
>   # Total indirect association for each message category
>   total_ind_choice01 := ind_hope_choice01 + ind_anxiety_choice01
>   total_ind_choice02 := ind_hope_choice02 + ind_anxiety_choice02
>   total_ind_choice03 := ind_hope_choice03 + ind_anxiety_choice03
>   total_ind_choice04 := ind_hope_choice04 + ind_anxiety_choice04
> 
>   # Total association: direct association plus the two indirect associations
>   total_effect_choice01 := c1 + total_ind_choice01
>   total_effect_choice02 := c2 + total_ind_choice02
>   total_effect_choice03 := c3 + total_ind_choice03
>   total_effect_choice04 := c4 + total_ind_choice04
>

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

However, much of this work typically relies on experimental designs in which participants are passively exposed to predefined message types selected by researchers, rather than being allowed to choose among messages, momentary feelings of anxiety may become incorporated into a broader climate-related anxious sentiment (Maran & Begotti, 2021; Shao & Yu, 2023).

A total of 291 participants were recruited from the United Kingdom through the Prolific platform.

Eight participants were excluded for failing the attention check or for not completing the task as instructed, resulting in a final sample of 283 participants (163 women, 113 men, 2 non-binary/third gender, 5 preferred not to say).

Ethical approval was obtained from the Ethical Review Board of the University of Amsterdam, and all participants provided informed consent prior to participation.

For example, for hopeful sentiment, participants were asked: When thinking about your own life situation in the next 20 years, to what extent do you feel hopeful regarding environmental issues?

After the baseline measurements, participants completed a selective exposure task adapted from Westerwick et al. (2017).

On an initial overview page, participants were presented with article headlines displayed as clickable rectangular buttons in a randomized grid layout.

Participants were informed that they had 10 minutes to browse the articles and were encouraged to read those they found most interesting.

To ensure sufficient data quality, participants were required to read at least four articles.

After the selective exposure task, participants completed a short memory test on the articles they had read.

Finally, participants provided demographic information, including age, gender, and education levels.

To select suitable experimental stimuli, we conducted a two-stage pilot study with UK-based participants recruited through Prolific.

Given that each participant provided multiple count-based responses (0/1/2) across experimental conditions, we employed Poisson mixed-effects models with random intercepts for participants to analyze participants’ selection behavior across various message types.

A total of 1,034 participants were recruited from the United Kingdom via the Prolific platform.

Ethical approval for this research was granted by the Ethical Review Board of the University of Amsterdam, and informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to participation

Next, participants completed the selective exposure task.

Forty-four participants (4.4%) selected no environmental articles.

Power Analysis Check

We used the LLM model ‘vllm/DeepSeek-V41-Flash-1017-FP8’ to check the contents of 3 paragraphs that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses.

All essential information could be detected.

power_type statistical_test sample_size alpha_level power effect_size effect_size_metric software
unknown other 1000 0.05 0.8 0.39 other simulation
text
To estimate the required sample size, a Monte Carlo power analysis was conducted based on the standardized path coefficients obtained from Study 1 (Muthén & Muthén, 2002) using the Monte Carlo Power Analysis for Indirect Effects web application (Schoemann et al., 2017). The simulation included 1,000 replications and 20,000 Monte Carlo draws per replication, with a target power of 0.80 and a 95% confidence level. Results indicated that the power to detect both indirect effects (via hopeful and anxious sentiments) reached target power at approximately N = 1,000, suggesting that a sample of around one thousand participants would be sufficient to reliably detect the mediation effects in this model.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

9c82y Our target sample size is set at 250 participants.
gz3be Detecting indirect effects generally requires larger sample sizes. Thus, based on the parallel mediation results from the exploratory study, we conducted a Monte Carlo power analysis specifically targeting the indirect effects. The simulation was conducted with 10,000 replications and 10,000 draws per replication, using the parameter estimates for the indirect effect paths obtained from the exploratory study. Assuming an alpha level of .05 and aiming for a statistical power of .80, the results indicated that a minimum of 950 participants is required to reliably detect the indirect effects.
Accordingly, we will recruit a sample of 1,000 participants in the confirmatory study to allow for potential exclusions.

research_questions People encounter a vast amount of information daily, but not all of it is received or processed. The behavior of preferentially engaging with specific information from the available options is known as selective exposure.
This study aims to investigate how selective exposure to environmental messages with varying valences influences individuals’ emotional stances (e.g., hope, optimism, anxiety, worry) toward environmental issues. Additionally, it explores whether the self-relevance of the messages moderates this effect.
Please refer to the “Conditions” and “Dependent Variable” sections for a comprehensive understanding of the study design.
This study includes the following hypotheses:
H1: The effects of selective exposure to environmental messages on emotional stances to this issue is influenced by message valence. Specifically:
• H1a: Exposure to positive environmental messages is expected to increase positive emotions toward this issue, such as hope and optimism.
• H1b: Exposure to negative environmental messages is expected to increase negative emotions towards this issue, such as anxiety and worry.
H2: The effects of selective exposure to environmental messages on emotional stances to this issue (both positive and negative) will be moderated by the self-relevance of the message, with stronger effects observed for human-related messages compared to animal-related messages. 		In a preregistered exploratory study(https://osf.io/9c82y), we employed a selective exposure paradigm to gain preliminary insights into how engagement with environmental messages of varying valence influences individuals’ emotional stances toward environmental issues, their subsequent information-seeking behaviors, and the moderating role of self-relevance in these processes. In the present confirmatory study, we adopt the same research design to attempt to replicate the findings from the exploratory study, and to test the following hypotheses:

Hypothesis 1:
In the environmental domain, exposure to negative messages is effective in changing people’s emotional stances toward environmental issues, and this effect is moderated by perceived self-relevance. Specifically:
H1a: Exposure to more self-relevant negative messages (e.g., human-related) is expected to result in a greater decrease in positive emotional stances, compared to less self-relevant messages (e.g., animal-related).
H1b: Exposure to more self-relevant negative messages (e.g., human-related) is expected to result in a greater increase in negative emotional stances, compared to less self-relevant messages (e.g., animal-related).

Hypothesis 2:
Exposure to negative human-related messages simultaneously influences information-seeking intentions through two opposing pathways, with emotional stances serving as mediators. Specifically:
H2a: Exposure to negative human-related messages is expected to decrease positive emotional stances, which in turn reduce information seeking intentions.
H2b: Exposure to negative human-related messages is expected to increase negative emotional stances, which in turn promote information seeking intentions.

Hypothesis 3:
Individuals with greater self-reported knowledge about environmental issues are more likely to select positive human-related messages. design_dependent_variables Describe the key dependent variable(s) specifying how they will be measured.
1. Selective Exposure
In our hypotheses, the indicators of selective exposure function as independent variables. However, we also explore several research questions where these indicators serve as dependent variables.
Selective exposure will be measured in the following way (Westerwick, Johnson, & Knobloch-Westerwick, 2017):
• Message selection: For each article, whether participants chose to read it or not (binary).
• Reading time: The duration (in seconds) spent reading each chosen article.
2. Change in Emotional Stance
Participants will report their emotional stances (hope, optimism, worry, anxiety) towards two societal issues (i.e., health and environment) both before and after the selective exposure task. For example, they will respond to items such as:
“When thinking about your own life situation in the next 20 years, to what extent do you feel [hopeful, optimistic, worried, anxious] regarding environmental issues?”
The increase in emotional stance will be calculated as the difference between the post-exposure and pre-exposure score. 		1. Selective Exposure
In our hypotheses, the indicators of selective exposure function as independent variables. However, we also explore several research questions where these indicators serve as dependent variables.
Selective exposure will be measured in the following way (Westerwick, Johnson, & Knobloch-Westerwick, 2017):
• Message selection: For each article, whether participants chose to read it or not (binary).
• Reading time: The duration (in seconds) spent reading each chosen article.
2. Emotional Stances
Participants will report their emotional stances (positive: hope, optimism; negative: worry, anxiety) towards environment issues both before and after the selective exposure task. For example, they will respond to items such as:
“When thinking about your own life situation in the next 20 years, to what extent do you feel [hopeful, optimistic, worried, anxious] regarding environmental issues?”

3. Perceived Knowledge
Participants will report their perceived knowledge about environmental issues, measured by a single item:
“How much do you currently know about environmental issues?”

4. Information Seeking Intention
In exploratory study, participants’ intentions to seek further information were measured using five items, following Kahlor (2010). The scale demonstrated excellent internal consistency (Cronbach’s α = .98), suggesting not only high reliability but also potential item redundancy. To keep the survey brief, we retained only one representative item in current study:
“I intend to find more information about environmental issues soon.”
This item showed the highest average inter-item correlation (r = .93), the highest signal-to-noise ratio and the lowest inter-item variance suggesting that it most accurately and consistently reflected the underlying construct (i.e., information-seeking intention). Responses will be measured on a 7-point Likert-type scale (1 = Strongly Disagree, 7 = Strongly Agree). 		Describe the key dependent variable(s) specifying how they will be measured.

study_design_overview In this study, participants are presented with a grid with 16 headlines of articles and are asked to choose those that they want to read. These articles with corresponding headlines serve as message materials. In addition to headlines/articles with environmental messages, participants can choose to read articles with health-related messages. Health messages serve as a distractor. The headlines/articles are structured using a 2 (valence: positive vs. negative content) × 2 (self-relevance: animal vs. human focus) × 2 (topic: health vs. environment) factorial design, resulting in eight conditions, each represented by a pair of headlines/articles.
For example, in the condition with positive valence, animal focus, and environmental topic, the article headlines are:
• Older elephants in East Africa face threats from climate change
• Higher temperatures threaten sea turtle hatchling production
Participants will be exposed to all 16 headlines at once. All article headlines will be displayed on an overview page, allowing participants to choose which articles they want to read. In the selective exposure task, participants are presented with a grid of article headlines and asked to choose which articles they would like to read. In addition to articles containing environmental messages, participants may also select articles related to health topics, which serve as control content.
The headline-article pairs are structured using a 2 (valence: positive vs. negative content) × 2 (self-relevance: animal vs. human focus) × 2 (topic: health vs. environment) factorial design, resulting in eight experimental conditions. Each condition includes two headline-article pairs.
For example, in the condition with positive valence and animal focus on environmental topics, the article headlines are:
• Older elephants in East Africa face threats from climate change
• Higher temperatures threaten sea turtle hatchling production

statistical_tests In this study, we adopt a fully exploratory data analysis approach to test our hypotheses and research questions (Ledgerwood, 2019).
Following the exploratory analysis and deriving preliminary conclusions, we plan to conduct a second, confirmatory study. This confirmatory study will preregister both hypotheses and the analysis plan to ensure transparency, rigor and robustness in our research process. 		For Hypothesis 1:
Following the approach of Westerwick et al. (2017), within each message condition (i.e., negative human-related condition), we will calculate the number of articles each participant chose to read. These counts will be used as four separate predictors in the analyses,
Controlling for baseline measures (i.e., pre-exposure positive and negative emotional stances) and other control variables (i.e., perceived knowledge, curiosity, interest, urgency), we will conduct separate regression analyses predicting post-exposure positive emotional stances and negative emotional stances.
Based on our hypotheses, selecting more negative human-related articles is expected to predict lower post-exposure positive emotions and higher post-exposure negative emotions more strongly than selecting negative animal-related articles.

For Hypothesis 2:
We will test a parallel mediation model, with four message selection variables (the same as for H1) simultaneously entered as the independent variables (X₁ to X₄), post-exposure positive emotional stances and negative emotional stances as two mediators (M₁ and M₂), and information-seeking intention as the dependent variable (Y). Baseline measures and other control variables (the same as for H1) will be included as covariates in the regression analyses.
Based on our hypotheses, exposure to more negative human-related messages is expected to lower positive emotion stances and raise negative emotion stances, which will respectively decrease and increase the intention to seek further information.

For Hypothesis 3:
Perceived knowledge will serve as the independent variable (IV), and positive human-related message selections will serve as the dependent variable (DV). Controlling baseline measures and other control variables (the same as for H1 and H2 except perceived knowledge), we will conduct Poisson regression analyses. A backward elimination method will be applied to reduce multicollinearity and to identify the most influential predictors.
Based on our hypotheses, participants who perceive themselves as more knowledgeable are expected to select mores positive human-related messages during the task. 		In this study, we adopt a fully exploratory data analysis approach to test our hypotheses and research questions (Ledgerwood, 2019).

sample_size Our target sample size is set at 250 participants. Detecting indirect effects generally requires larger sample sizes. Thus, based on the parallel mediation results from the exploratory study, we conducted a Monte Carlo power analysis specifically targeting the indirect effects. The simulation was conducted with 10,000 replications and 10,000 draws per replication, using the parameter estimates for the indirect effect paths obtained from the exploratory study. Assuming an alpha level of .05 and aiming for a statistical power of .80, the results indicated that a minimum of 950 participants is required to reliably detect the indirect effects.
Accordingly, we will recruit a sample of 1,000 participants in the confirmatory study to allow for potential exclusions. 		Our target sample size is set at 250 participants. Accordingly, we will recruit a sample of 1,000 participants in the confirmatory study to allow for potential exclusions.
name An exploratory study on selective exposure to environmental messages A confirmatory study on selective exposure to environmental messages An exploratory study on selective exposure to environmental messages A confirmatory study on selective exposure to environmental messages
type_of_project Survey Survey Survey Survey
additional_comments Exploratory purposes
1. In our hypotheses, we predict how environmental message features, such as valence and self-relevance, might impact emotional stances. Additionally, we are interested in Exploratory Question 1: Do message features affect people’s engagement preferences?
Specifically:
• Do people prefer environmental messages or health messages?
• … positive messages or negative messages?
• … human-related messages or animal-related messages?
2. We also collect other variables that might explain preferences for environmental messages, such as baseline (pre-exposure) emotional stances (i.e., hope, optimism, anxiety, and worry), as well as other motivational factors such as interest, curiosity, urgency, and perceived knowledge regarding environmental issues.
Exploratory Question 2: Do emotional stances, interest, curiosity, urgency, and perceived knowledge regarding environmental issues influence people’s selective exposure to environmental messages?
For example, curiosity will be measured with the item: “When thinking about the current state of the world in terms of environmental issues, how curious do you feel?”
3. We are interested in whether exposure to environmental messages influences the intention to seek further environmental information.
Exploratory Question 3: Does greater selective exposure to environmental messages leads to a stronger intention to seek information?
Information seeking intention will be measured by 5 items, such as: I plan to seek information about environmental issues in the near future” (Kahlor, 2010).
4. We aim to explore whether increases in emotional stances — both positive and negative — are associated with the intention to seek further environmental information.
Exploratory Question 4: Do increases in hope, optimism, anxiety, or worry towards environmental issues relate to the intention to seek environmental information, serving as a mediator between selective exposure and information-seeking behavior?

Article questions
We designed multiple-choice questions with three options tailored to the content of each article to explore the extent to which participants read the articles. Based on participants’ reading selections, these questions will be presented randomly after the task, with up to three questions. This approach could serve as a possible attention check in follow-up studies to assess whether participants carefully read the articles they chose.

References
Kahlor, L. (2010). PRISM: a planned risk information seeking model. Health Commun, 25(4), 345-356. doi:10.1080/10410231003775172
Ledgerwood, A. (2019). New developments in research methods. Advanced social psychology.
Westerwick, A., Johnson, B. K., & Knobloch-Westerwick, S. (2017). Change Your Ways: Fostering Health Attitudes Toward Change Through Selective Exposure to Online Health Messages. Health Commun, 32(5), 639-649. doi:10.1080/10410236.2016.1160319 		1. In the exploratory study, the two selective exposure indicators — message selection and reading time — showed similar patterns of results. Therefore, in the confirmatory study, we will focus on message selection as the primary indicator. Findings related to reading time will be examined for exploratory purposes and reported as supplementary results.
2. We also collect the same set of data for health-related issues to examine whether the hypothesized relationships hold within the health domain.
3. Beyond the findings specifically related to negative human-related messages, we also explore the effects of other message types—namely, positive human-related messages, negative animal-related messages and positive animal-related messages. Specifically, we will explore whether 1) these messages influence participants’ emotional stances toward environmental issues (i.e., similar to the effect proposed in H1); 2) this process subsequently influences participants’ intentions to seek further environmental information (i.e., as proposed in H2); and 3) perceived knowledge, baseline emotional stances or other factors (curiosity, interest, and urgency) predict participants’ selection of these messages.
4. Building on the procedure used in the exploratory study, we collected participants’ levels of curiosity, interest, and urgency toward environmental issues prior to the selective exposure task as control variables. In the confirmatory study, these variables will also be measured after the task to explore potential changes. This allows us to explore, for example, whether exposure to negative human-related messages may increase participants’ curiosity, interest, or urgency regarding environmental issues.
5. Finally, four open-ended questions will be included to investigate participants’ motivations for engaging with, or avoiding, positive and negative environmental content (e.g., news articles, documentaries, expositions, books).

Analyses related to purposes 4 will be conducted using an exploratory data analysis approach (Ledgerwood, 2019). The data collected with the open-ended questions will be analyzed using a qualitative strategy. 		Exploratory purposes
