How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

A paper that states that no human or animal subjects took part (“no human subjects were involved”, “did not involve human participants”, or people taking part “not as subjects”) is not expected to have an ethics statement, whatever participant phrase it also has (see .detect_no_participants()). A negation near a participant phrase alone (“No participants were excluded”) does not count: it reports a study with participants.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold” or “legend”). Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Levi Baruch

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Environmental problems are intensifying, prompting expanded public communication efforts to raise awareness and motivate pro-environmental behavior. However, meaningful engagement with environmental messages is often selective, as people actively choose among many competing messages.

In this paper, we examined how active engagement with environmental messages related to affective orientations (i.e., sentiments) towards environmental issues. Through a selective exposure paradigm, participants selected from four types of environmental messages varying in valence (positive vs. negative) and personal relevance (human vs. animal). We expected that engagement with these messages would be associated with changes in hopeful and anxious sentiments toward environmental issues. These sentiment shifts, in turn, were expected to predict the likelihood of participants seeking further environmental information. In an initial exploratory study (N = 283), participants' selection of the different kinds of environmental messages showed no direct effect on environmental information-seeking intentions.

Further analyses revealed two competing indirect paths: (a) increased seeking intentions via enhanced anxious sentiments and (b) reduced seeking intentions via diminished hopeful sentiments. These patterns were replicated in a confirmatory study (N = 1,009), demonstrating their robustness. Together, these findings suggest that the effectiveness of environmental communication is not limited to valencecongruent sentiments. Instead, the balance of emotional reactions that messages trigger shapes information-seeking behavior.

1. Introduction

Environmental problems, including extreme weather, biodiversity loss, and ocean pollution, are getting worse (UNEP, 2025), threatening both ecosystems and human well-being (Nesmith et al., 2021; Yang, 2025). Environmental communication plays a crucial role in sustaining public attention to climate and ecological crises (Ter Mors et al., 2010). However, greater access to information doesn't always translate into more action addressing a societal problem (Ejaz et al., 2025). A growing number of studies are exploring which message features are most effective in attracting attention and encouraging engagement with environmental issues, with the ultimate goal of creating better environmental communication strategies to drive behavior change.

Building on this work, the present research uses a selective exposure paradigm to investigate people's active choices among different environmental messages. Across two studies, participants chose among positive and negative environmental messages that focused on consequences for either humans or animals, with human-focused messages designed to be more personally relevant. To examine the implications of these choices, we assessed changes in participants' broader affective evaluations of environmental issues, which we conceptualize as sentiments, as well as their subsequent informationseeking intentions. We expected participants' message choices to be associated with changes in hopeful and anxious sentiments. We also tested whether these sentiments predicted subsequent intentions to seek further environmental information.

1.1. Selective Exposure as a Measure of Active Choice

Without exposure, media messages cannot produce any effects on audiences (McGuire, 1985).

Accordingly, examining the effects of messages requires consideration of whether and how individuals engage with the content available to them. Prior research has shown that message features such as valence and personal relevance shape audience responses, including risk perception and pro-environmental intentions (Jacobson et al., 2019; Rosenthal & Ai, 2024; Scannell & Gifford, 2013; Troy et al., 2024).

However, much of this work typically relies on experimental designs in which participants are passively exposed to predefined message types selected by researchers, rather than being allowed to choose among messages, momentary feelings of anxiety may become incorporated into a broader climate-related anxious sentiment (Maran & Begotti, 2021; Shao & Yu, 2023). Likewise, repeated exposure to hope appeals in environmental communications may evoke momentary hopeful responses, which can gradually consolidate into more stable hopeful sentiment that encourages engagement with environmental problems (Chadwick, 2015). Thus, individuals may come to hold relatively stable sentiments toward environmental issues. These sentiments may influence not only how environmental issues are perceived, but also individuals' openness to further information engagement (Kahlor, 2010). This makes sentiment a particularly useful lens for understanding the broader affective implications of selective engagement with environmental messages.

1.3. Message Characteristics in Environmental Communication

To examine how people's message choices may relate to environmental sentiments, we focus on two key attributes of environmental messages: valence and personal relevance. Message valence carries the "emotional charge" of environmental news, labeling it as either a warning of damage or a sign of (potential) success. Negative valence centers on the breakdown of ecosystems, threats, and harm, whereas positive valence highlights recovery and effective environmental action. Environmental communication is often dominated by negative messages, which can heighten risk perception and awareness (Diamond & Urbanski, 2022; Troy et al., 2024). However, when such messages emphasize adverse impacts without offering actionable solutions, they may elicit defensive responses or information avoidance (Brosch, 2021; Ettinger et al., 2021). Scholars have therefore advocated for more positive, solution-oriented approaches, such as hope-based communication, which highlight efficacy and actionable pathways (Chadwick, 2015; Troy et al., 2024). Evidence suggests that these approaches can increase interest in climate protection and pro-environmental intentions (Baden et al., 2019; Chadwick, 2015). Together, these studies suggest that message valence is related to how audiences perceive and respond to environmental information.

A second important message attribute is personal relevance, which refers to the extent to which information connects to individuals' self-concept, goals, values, or lived experiences (Petty & Cacioppo, 1986; Schäfer et al., 2020). In general, information perceived as more personally relevant tends to attract more attention and deeper processing (Arlt et al., 2018; El Hedhli & Zourrig, 2023; Liu & Yang, 2023). In the environmental domain, climate change is more likely to attract attention and engagement when it is perceived as a personal rather than merely societal threat (Ma et al., 2023). Similarly, environmental issues that are experienced as geographically close rather than distant tend to elicit higher risk perceptions and more intense emotional responses (Mărgărint et al., 2021; Milfont et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2025).

Taken together, findings on message valence and personal relevance suggest that both may be related to engagement with environmental information and how it is perceived and experienced. We reasoned that, in a selective exposure context, the valence and personal relevance of the messages people select may therefore be related to their subsequent environmental sentiments.

1.4. The Current Study

The primary aim of the current study was to examine how selective engagement with environmental messages relates to changes in sentiments toward environmental issues, as well as whether these sentiments would predict information-seeking intentions. We expected that the relationship between participants' selective exposure to environmental messages and their sentiments, that is, their affective orientation towards environmental issues, would vary by message valence (H1). Specifically, selective exposure to positive environmental messages was expected to be associated with increases in hopeful and optimistic sentiments (H1a), whereas selective exposure to negative environmental messages was expected to be associated with increases in anxious and worried sentiments (H1b).

Furthermore, affective responses toward societal issues depend on how people view an event's relevance to their own concerns and goals (Brosch, 2021; Moors et al., 2013). Accordingly, sentiments toward environmental issues elicited by climate-related messages may depend on the extent to which individuals see such messages as personally relevant. Building on this perspective, we hypothesized that the relationship between selective exposure to environmental messages and sentiments (hopeful, optimistic, anxious, and worried) toward environmental issues would be moderated by the personal relevance of the message, with stronger associations for highly relevant messages than for less personally relevant messages (H2).

Finally, beyond sentiments, we were interested in the behavioral implications of exposure to environmental messages, particularly in terms of individuals' intentions to seek further environmental information. This could form a dynamic feedback loop in which initial message exposure is linked to information seeking, which may in turn be associated with further exposure to environmental messages.

Based on prior theories and empirical research on information seeking, affective responses such as feelings of threat, worry and hope, play a central role in motivating information-seeking intentions (Kahlor, 2010; Yang & Kahlor, 2012), including in environmental contexts (Choo, 2023; Kahlor et al., 2020). As broader, issue-specific affective orientations, sentiments may similarly serve as predictors of information-seeking intentions.

However, existing literature offers less clear guidance on whether sentiments are likely to motivate further information seeking, and if so, in what direction. Accordingly, we posed the following research question: How are post-exposure sentiments, both hopeful and anxious, associated with individuals' intentions to seek further environmental information (RQ)?

In this paper, we adopted a stepwise exploratory-confirmatory approach to address our hypotheses and research question. The exploratory study was conducted to provide an initial test of the hypothesized model and to identify potential relationships among key variables. The results were then used to inform power calculations and sample size estimation for a subsequent confirmatory study (Button et al., 2013). This separation into exploratory and confirmatory phases also serves to assess the reproducibility of the findings (Oberauer & Lewandowsky, 2019). 1 Conceptual Model 2 3 Note. The dashed box represents participants' active choice of environmental messages; participants 4 could select messages from multiple categories. "++" and "+" indicate hypothesized positive associations 5 between message selections and the corresponding environmental sentiments (H1a and H1b), with "++" 6 indicating stronger associations for messages with higher personal relevance (H2). Paths from 7 environmental sentiments to subsequent information-seeking intentions represent research questions for 8 which no directional hypotheses were specified.

9 10 ++ Positive environmental sentiment (e.g., hope, optimism) Negative environmental sentiment (e.g., anxiety, worry) Positive, highly personally relevant environmental messages Negative, highly personally relevant environmental messages Environmental information-seeking intentions ++ Participants' active choices (selective exposure) Negative, less personally relevant environmental messages + Positive, less personally relevant environmental messages + 2. Study 1 (Exploratory) 2.1. Method

2.1.1. Pre-registration

The exploratory study was pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF; https://osf.io/9c82y/overview?view_only=4f21d42b9fd14843b2e20b2e3219870a). In this preregistration, Hypotheses 1 and 2 were pre-registered as confirmatory because prior theory and empirical work offered clear support for directional predictions; the additional research question concerning future informationseeking intentions was specified as exploratory. Regarding the analysis plan, we adopted a fully exploratory data-analytic approach to test the hypotheses and the research question in the exploratory study (Ledgerwood, 2019); the final analysis strategy was subsequently carried forward and directly applied in the confirmatory study. Results for additional exploratory questions preregistered on OSF are reported in the Supplementary Materials.

2.1.2. Participants

A total of 291 participants were recruited from the United Kingdom through the Prolific platform.

Eight participants were excluded for failing the attention check or for not completing the task as instructed, resulting in a final sample of 283 participants (163 women, 113 men, 2 non-binary/third gender, 5 preferred not to say). Participants ranged in age from 18 to 83 years (M = 37.42, SD = 12.52).

Most participants held at least a bachelor's degree (38.9% bachelor's, 23.3% graduate or professional). As Study 1 was exploratory, the sample size was guided by previous research on selective exposure rather than by an a-priori power analysis (Luong et al., 2021). Participants received 2.70 UK pounds for completing the study, which took approximately 18 minutes.

Ethical approval was obtained from the Ethical Review Board of the University of Amsterdam, and all participants provided informed consent prior to participation. A content warning was included to specify that some of the articles included negative content.

2.1.3. Procedure and Measures

The overall procedure is illustrated in Figure 2A.

2.1.3.1. Baseline.

Sentiments. Before the selective exposure task, participants reported their baseline sentiments toward environmental issues. Sentiment was conceptualized as an affective orientation that integrates discrete emotional experiences with a relatively enduring evaluative attitude towards a specific issue. The present study operationalized this construct through four emotions felt towards environmental issues in the context of their future consequences. Worry and anxiety captured persistent concern about environmental risks (Bechtoldt & Schermelleh-Engel, 2025; Maran & Begotti, 2021; Verplanken et al., 2020), whereas hope and optimism reflected sustained expectations for environmental improvement (Lee et al., 2017; McAfee et al., 2019; Zeier et al., 2025). These emotions were selected to represent distinct yet complementary sentiments toward environmental issues.

Each sentiment was assessed using a single-item, 100-point scale ranging from 1 (not at all) and 100 (extremely). For example, for hopeful sentiment, participants were asked: When thinking about your own life situation in the next 20 years, to what extent do you feel hopeful regarding environmental issues?

Because environmental issues often involve long-term risks and prospects for improvement, the 20-year framing anchored participants' current feelings within this longer-term horizon. The items therefore assessed participants' current sentiments toward environmental issues in the context of their longer-term personal future, rather than how they expected to feel in the future. To minimize potential order effects, the presentation order of the four sentiments was counterbalanced across participants following a Latinsquare design.

Control Variables.

We measured several control variables, namely curiosity, interest, urgency, and perceived knowledge regarding environmental issues. These variables were included to account for individual differences in baseline engagement and motivation. All items were assessed on 100-point scales ranging from 0 (not at all) to 100 (extremely). Item wordings are reported in the Supplementary Materials.

2.1.3.2. Selective Exposure Task.

After the baseline measurements, participants completed a selective exposure task adapted from Westerwick et al. (2017). On an initial overview page, participants were presented with article headlines displayed as clickable rectangular buttons in a randomized grid layout. Participants were informed that they had 10 minutes to browse the articles and were encouraged to read those they found most interesting. To ensure sufficient data quality, participants were required to read at least four articles. Clicking a headline opened a pop-up window with the full article text, formatted in a newspaper-style layout. After reading the article, participants closed the pop-up window and returned to the overview page to select another article. The headline selection and article reading screens are shown in Figure 2B.

During the task, participants could read new articles, revisit previously read articles, or, when a minimum of four articles were chosen, decide not to read further. Participants' article selections were tracked in real time using JavaScript-based monitoring. Following Wojcieszak (2021), we measured exposure as the number of articles selected within each messages type. The task automatically terminated after 10 minutes, redirecting participants to the next section of the study.

Two instructed response items were included as attention checks, with one placed before and one after the selective exposure task. For instance, one item said To ensure you are paying attention, please select option C below. Participants who failed one or more attention checks were excluded from the analysis.

2.1.3.3. Post-exposure.

Memory Test. After the selective exposure task, participants completed a short memory test on the articles they had read. The test consisted of three multiple-choice questions, each with three response options, based on a randomly drawn subset of the articles chosen by each participant. This measure served as an indicator of participants' engagement with the content.

Post-exposure Sentiments and Information-Seeking Intentions.

Participants then reported their sentiments toward environmental issues again, using the same items and response format as the baseline measurement. Then, participants reported their intentions to seek further information about environmental topics, assessed using a five-item measure adapted from Kahlor (2010) (e.g., "I intend to find more information about environmental issues soon"). Responses were recorded on a 7-point scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). Finally, participants provided demographic information, including age, gender, and education levels.

2.1.4.1. Pilot Testing and Selection of Stimuli.

To select suitable experimental stimuli, we conducted a two-stage pilot study with UK-based participants recruited through Prolific. We manipulated the personal relevance of messages by contrasting human-and animal-focused messages. This approach builds on the fact that environmental degradation affects both human and animal welfare (Shivanna, 2022), allowing us to identify suitable stimulus material from real-world news sources. Health-related articles were included alongside the environmental articles as a control condition. The materials were thus designed to vary systematically across three manipulated dimensions: Valence (positive vs. negative), Relevance (human vs. animal), and Topic (environment vs. health), while being match in terms of levels of interest, comprehensibility, and headline-article consistency.

Online news reports were selected from English-language outlets such as Euronews and Science Daily to provide a realistic context for participants' selective exposure decisions. All texts were carefully edited to be 160-190 words long, ensuring that each could be read in under one minute given an average reading speed of ~200 words per minute (Rayner et al., 2016). Each article was paired with a headline, which was either adapted from the original source or newly generated to match the intended valence and personal relevance of the message.

Because the participants in the main study would choose which articles to read based on the headlines, the pilot study measured the attributes they expected the articles to have based on the headline, in terms of positivity, negativity, human focus, animal focus, environmental focus, and health focus.

These ratings also served to assess whether the intended manipulations were clearly conveyed by the headlines themselves. For example, for each headline, participants rated how positive they expected an article associated with this headline to be. The extent to which the articles reflected the attributes implied by the headlines was assessed through participants' post-reading ratings of headline-article consistency, based on two items: "How adequately does the article match the headline?" and "How well does the headline summarize the article?" Higher consistency ratings indicated greater alignment between the headline and article content.

The stimulus set was validated in a two-stage pilot study, (𝑁 !" #$%& = 45, 𝑁 !" #$%' = 44). Because the results the human-related materials did not perform satisfactorily in Stage 1, we selected and tested a revised set of candidate materials in Stage 2. Based on the pilot study, we selected 16 articles: two for each combination of valence, relevance and topic type. The selected articles were comparable in length (M = 178.31 words, SD = 7.92; range = 165-189 words), and the headlines were also similar in length (M = 7.81 words, SD = 1.56; range = 6-10 words). For example, environmental articles included humanfocused positive stories such as Clean Energy Tech Slows Global Carbon Emissions Growth and animalfocused negative stories such as Older Elephants in East Africa Face Threats from Climate Change. The full list of article titles is provided in the Supplementary Materials.

Manipulation checks confirmed the intended distinctions. All environmental headlines were considered as more environment-related than health-related (𝑀 %()*+,(-%(" > 69.69, 𝑀 . %#/". < 42.13, ps<.001). Positive headlines were rated as more positive than negative headlines (𝑀 0,! *"*)% > 69.96, 𝑀 (%$#"*)% < 23.86, ps<.001), whereas negative headlines were rated as more negative (𝑀 (%$#"*)% > 67.48, 𝑀 0,! *"*)% < 26.66, ps<.001) than positive headlines. These results indicate that the valence manipulation was successful. The relevance manipulation also worked as intended: Human-related headlines received higher ratings on human relevance than animal-related headlines (𝑀 .1-#( > 58.57, 𝑀 #(*-#/ < 23.61, ps<.001), whereas animal-related articles received higher ratings on animal relevance than human-related headlines (𝑀 #(*-#/ > 89.82, 𝑀 .1-#( < 21.02, ps<.001). Further details about stimulus selection and pretesting are provided in the Supplementary Materials.

2.1.4.2. Assessment of Personal Relevance Manipulation.

To verify that the human-animal manipulation effectively influenced perceived personal relevance, participants rated each headline on the item "To what extent do you expect that the article with this headline will be personally relevant to you?" on a 0-100 scale. Because each condition included two articles, a linear mixed-effects model was fitted to account for potential material-specific influences, with random intercepts for participants and articles and fixed effects for Relevance (human vs. animal) and Valence (positive vs. negative).

The analysis revealed a significant main effect of Relevance, β = 32.81, SE = 4.92, t(22.74) = 6.66, p < .001, indicating that participants rated human-related articles as significantly more personally relevant than animal-related ones. This effect was qualified by a significant Relevance × Valence interaction (β = -20.03, SE = 4.31, t(3.96) = -4.64, p = .010), which suggested that the difference in perceived personal relevance between human-and animal-related messages was smaller for positive articles.

Simple-effects analyses confirmed that human-related articles were rated significantly higher in personal relevance than animal-related ones, both in the negative condition (t(22.9) = 6.66, p < .001) and the positive condition (t(22.9) = 2.60, p = .016), confirming that the human-animal manipulation successfully affected perceived personal relevance.

2.1.5. Analytic Strategy

Our hypotheses focused exclusively on exposure to environmental articles, and we therefore limit our reported analyses to the environmental domain.

Before examining the hypotheses and research question, we conducted variable aggregation.

Correlation analyses revealed that, both pre-and post-exposure, the hopeful sentiment was strongly correlated with the optimistic sentiment (𝑟 0+% = 0.85, p < .001; 𝑟 0,!" = 0.88, p<.001), and the worried sentiment with the anxious sentiment (𝑟 0+% = 0.81, p < .001; 𝑟 0,!" = 0.83, p < .001). These high correlations suggested that each pair conceptually reflected a shared underlying affective dimension. We therefore aggregated them into composite scores of hopeful sentiment (hope and optimism) and anxious sentiment (anxiety and worry). Similarly, since interest and curiosity were highly correlated (r = 0.96, p < .001), they were combined into a single composite score of interest.

We adapted the analytic strategy described by Westerwick et al. (2017). Participants' selections of the four environmental message types (positive-human, negative-human, positive-animal, and negativeanimal) were entered simultaneously as predictors in two separate regression analyses, with post-exposure hopeful environmental sentiment and anxious environmental sentiment serving as the dependent variables, respectively. Baseline measures of pre-exposure environmental sentiments, as well as interest, urgency, and perceived knowledge about environmental issues, were included as control variables.

This approach allowed Hypotheses 1 and 2 to be examined within the same models. H1a was assessed by examining whether selections of positive-human and positive-animal messages were associated with higher post-exposure hopeful sentiment, whereas H1b was assessed by examining whether selections of negative-human and negative-animal messages were associated with higher postexposure anxious sentiment. To test whether these associations differed by personal relevance (H2), we conducted linear hypothesis tests comparing the regression coefficients for human-and animal-related message selections, separately within the positive and negative message conditions and within each sentiment model. These tests evaluated whether the two corresponding regression coefficients differed significantly and yielded the reported F statistics. Thus, personal relevance was examined through coefficient comparisons rather than by including a conventional product-term interaction. This strategy allowed participants' mixed selection patterns to be represented within a single participant-level model. It also enabled the association of each message category with post-exposure sentiment to be estimated while accounting for selections from the other categories.

Next, we addressed the research question concerning how post-exposure sentiments would predict participants' subsequent environmental information-seeking intentions. As post-exposure sentiments were expected to be associated with the types of messages participants chose to engage with, we specified a structural equation model with parallel indirect pathways to comprehensively map these relationships. In this model, paths were specified from environmental message selection to post-exposure hopeful and anxious environmental sentiments, and from these sentiments to environmental informationseeking intentions, while controlling for baseline sentiments and other covariates. All four message types (positive-human, negative-human, positive-animal, and negative-animal) were entered simultaneously as predictors to estimate their unique associations while accounting for shared variance across message categories. Direct paths from message selection to information-seeking intentions were included for model completeness and were consistent with the preregistered exploratory objective. The model was conducted in R (R Core Team, 2023) using the lavaan package (Rosseel, 2012).

2.2. Results

>Results

2.2.1. Memory Test

Memory performance was examined as a descriptive indicator of participants' processing of the selected articles. Of the participants, 51.24% answered all three memory questions correctly, 34.28% answered two correctly, 13.07% answered one correctly, and 1.41% answered none correctly. These descriptives suggest that most participants retained at least some information from the article content.

Participants with lower memory performance were retained in the main analyses because the selective exposure design was intended to approximate naturalistic information engagement, where variation in attention and message processing is expected. As a sensitivity analysis, we excluded participants who answered none of the memory questions correctly; this yielded substantively unchanged results, and we therefore report the full-sample analyses.

2.2.2. Message Choice Patterns in Selective Exposure

On average, participants selected 7.40 (SD = 3.42) out of 16 available articles overall, including 3.50 (SD = 2.18) out of eight environmental messages, demonstrating that the browsing task allowed for selectivity in reading. Given that each participant provided multiple count-based responses (0/1/2) across experimental conditions, we employed Poisson mixed-effects models with random intercepts for participants to analyze participants' selection behavior across various message types. The results revealed a significant valence × personal relevance interaction, b = -0.44, SE = 0.13, z = -3.45, p < .001, indicating that participants' preference for positive versus negative messages differed between human-related and animal-related messages. We conducted Bonferroni-adjusted post-hoc pairwise comparisons of estimated marginal means. Under negative valence, participants' selections did not differ between human-related (M = 0.86, SD = 0.83) and animal-related messages (M = 0.70, SD = 0.76), z = -2.10, p = .072. Conversely, under positive valence, participants selected more animal-related (M = 1.08, SD = 0.78) than humanrelated messages (M = 0.85, SD = 0.78), z = 2.83, p = .009.

Participants' environmental message selections were generally mixed across both message dimensions. Most chose both positive and negative articles (n = 193, 68.2%), but 63 people (22.3%) chose only positive articles and 17 (6.0%) chose only negative articles. In terms of personal relevance, 180 participants (63.6%) selected both human-and animal-related articles, while 38 participants (13.4%) selected only human-related articles and 55 (19.4%) selected only animal-related articles. Considering the two dimensions together, 153 participants (54.1%) made selections that included both valences and both personal-relevance categories. Ten participants (3.5%) selected no environmental articles. Supplementary Materials provide a detailed breakdown of these selection patterns by valence and personal relevance.

We also examined whether baseline sentiments, interest, urgency, and perceived knowledge were associated with message selection. The full results are reported in the Supplementary Materials.

2.2.3. Associations Between Selective Exposure and Environmental Sentiments

Table 1 summarizes the results of regression analyses predicting post-exposure environmental sentiments.

2.2.3.1. Hypothesis 1a.

Hypothesis 1a predicted that greater exposure to positive environmental messages would be associated with higher hopeful environmental sentiment. However, the coefficient for positive human-related message selections was positive but only marginally significant (β = 0.08, t(273) = 1.75, p = .081, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.18]). The coefficient for positive animal-related message selections was not statistically significant either (β = -0.05, t(273) = -1.13, p = .262, 95% CI [-0.14, 0.04]). Thus, Hypothesis 1a was not supported. At the same time, participants who selected more negative humanrelated messages reported significantly lower post-exposure hopeful environmental sentiment (β = -0.15, t(273) = -3.06, p = .002, 95% CI [-0.24, -0.05]), whereas the coefficient for negative animal-related message selections was not statistically significant (β = 0.005, t(273) = 0.10, p = .921, 95% CI [-0.09, 0.10]).

2.2.3.2. Hypothesis 1b.

Hypothesis 1b predicted that greater exposure to negative environmental messages would correspond to higher anxious environmental sentiment. Consistent with the hypothesis, negative human-related message selections were a significant positive predictor of anxious environmental sentiment (β = 0.09, t(273) = 2.51, p = .013, 95% CI [0.02, 0.17]). However, the coefficient for negative animal-related message selections was positive but only marginally significant (β = 0.07, t(273) = 1.90, p = .059, 95% CI [-0.003, 0.14]). Thus, Hypothesis 1b received partial support. Additionally, participants who selected more positive human-related messages also reported significantly lower anxious environmental sentiment (β = -0.08, t(273) = -2.09, p = .037, 95% CI [-0.15, -0.004]), while positive animal-related message selections were not significantly related to anxious environmental sentiment (β = 0.02, t(273) = 0.61, p = .545, 95% CI [-0.05, 0.09]).

2.2.3.3. Hypothesis 2. Hypothesis 2 predicted that personal relevance (human vs. animal) would moderate

the associations between participants' environmental message selections and their environmental sentiments. Regression coefficient comparisons showed that, in the model predicting hopeful environmental sentiment, positive human-related message selections were significantly stronger predictors of higher hopeful sentiment than were positive animal-related message selections, F(1,273) = 3.91, p = .049. For negative messages, human-related selections were more negatively associated with hopeful sentiment than animal-related selections, F(1, 273) = 4.12, p = .043. In the model predicting anxious environmental sentiment, positive human-related selections were more negatively associated with anxious sentiment than positive animal-related selections, although the difference was marginally significant, F(1,273) = 3.50, p = .063. Negative human-and animal-related message selections did not differ significantly in predicting higher anxious sentiment, F(1,273) = 0.17, p = .678.

Taken together, the results for self-selected exposure provided little support for Hypothesis 1a and partial support for Hypothesis 1b. Positive environmental message selections were not significant predictors of hopeful sentiment, whereas participants who selected more negative human-related messages reported significantly higher anxious sentiment. Evidence for Hypothesis 2 was mixed. In the model predicting hopeful sentiment, human-related selections had a more positive association than animal-related selections for positive messages and a more negative association for negative messages.

For anxious sentiment, the human-animal difference was marginal for positive messages and nonsignificant for negative messages.

2.2.4. Associations Between Environmental Sentiments and Environmental Information-Seeking Intentions

To address the research question of how post-exposure sentiments would predict participants' subsequent environmental information-seeking intentions, we conducted a parallel mediation analysis.

Specifically, hopeful and anxious post-exposure sentiments were included simultaneously as mediators linking message selection to information-seeking intentions, while controlling for their corresponding preexposure levels. The structure and standardized path coefficients of the model are presented in Figure 3.

The overall pattern of paths between message selections and post-exposure sentiments was consistent with the preceding regression analyses.

Neither the estimated direct nor total effects of environmental message selections on informationseeking intentions were statistically significant. However, both post-exposure hopeful and anxious environmental sentiments positively predicted information-seeking intentions.

Significant indirect effects were found only for negative human-related message selections.

Specifically, participants who selected more negative human-related messages reported higher anxious sentiment, which positively predicted information-seeking intentions. The estimated indirect effect via anxious sentiment was therefore positive. These participants also reported lower hopeful sentiment.

Because hopeful sentiment positively predicted information-seeking intentions, the estimated indirect effect via hopeful sentiment was negative. Thus, the parallel mediation model showed two opposing indirect associations linking self-selected exposure to negative human-related messages with informationseeking intentions, although the total effect was not significant.

2.3. Discussion

The results from Study 1 indicate that participants' post-exposure environmental sentiments were related to the environmental articles they actively chose to read, particularly in response to negative, highly personally relevant messages. Specifically, participants who selected more negative human-related messages reported higher anxious sentiment and lower hopeful sentiment. These contrasting patterns may help account for the nonsignificant overall association between selective exposure to these messages and information-seeking intentions. The parallel mediation analysis estimated a positive indirect effect via anxious sentiment and a negative indirect effect via hopeful sentiment. This pattern deserves further investigation, as it may help explain why communication strategies that emphasize a single emotional valence may yield limited behavioral effects: they may focus on strengthening one sentiment while overlooking changes in another sentiment that differentially affect information seeking.

In addition, the moderating role of personal relevance in the relationship between message exposure and sentiments received only partial support. The failure to reach statistical significance may be due to the limited statistical power given the relatively small sample size of the exploratory study (Button et al., 2013). Nevertheless, the pattern of coefficient differences suggested generally stronger relationships for human-related than for animal-related message selections, consistent with prior empirical findings (Arlt et al., 2018; Liu & Yang, 2023), and so we considered it worthwhile to test this in a confirmatory study with a larger sample size.
